Customer preparation

AI can change a profession through its customers. People arrive with more work completed, different questions, and new reasons to seek advice. Professional demand then changes even when practitioners keep their own tools and procedures. We study this indirect route because the economic effects of AI extend beyond the workplace where it is used.

Our question concerns what happens over time. Work completed today also trains the people who will supply expertise tomorrow. When their expertise contributes to research, customer choices can reach the production of new AI. Future capabilities then return to customers and researchers, connecting professional change to technological progress (fig. 1).

We follow this connection through the choices of customers, workers, and a research fund. Each responds to a price or an expected return, and their choices determine what work is done and who learns from it. Bringing those decisions together lets us trace an immediate saving into its later consequences.

Work and learning

We treat experience as something conveyed by the information a worker actually receives. Completing a service and learning from it are distinct outcomes, so a change in working hours can carry a different change in future ability. This distinction allows customer preparation to affect both current production and the formation of expertise.

Workers own the qualifications they acquire and can carry them to another employer. We connect learning opportunities to future earnings, and place their financing alongside the customer’s fee and the cost of formal instruction. This gives experience a price and makes the supply of expertise respond to the work people expect to do.

Key findings

Learning opportunities can lower service fees when workers can pay for the experience they gain. Customers then face part of the future cost of displacing that experience. Restrictions on learning payments weaken this connection, making the rules for financing training relevant to the customer’s preparation choice.

More formal training can accompany fewer experts. In our comparison with demand for remaining expert work held fixed, formal instruction replaces only part of the lost practice. Rising training effort can thus be a response to lost workplace learning while the eventual expert workforce becomes smaller.

Research can gain time immediately and lose expertise later. Under human research, its eventual labor depends on the service hours released relative to the expert supply lost, evaluated at the old wage and training incentive. This connects customer efficiency to the future capacity for innovation. When methods mix at equal cost, their shares can adjust while the budget purchases the same output.

Smaller bills and greater social value can move differently. Expertise that supports further research can be worth more to society than to its holder. Customer preparation then has to be valued through both the learning it displaces and the expert time that reaches research, alongside its private saving.

Recursive improvement

Research uses current AI to help produce future AI. We call this recursive self-improvement, or RSI. People can carry the process by using AI throughout their research, and a feasible autonomous method can carry it through computation. Including both routes lets us ask how much technological progress continues to depend on human expertise.

Each route must complete generation and validation, and each advance takes time to become useful in later research. We include these requirements when following the recursion. They determine how the customer and career mechanisms operate within a growing economy, and why faster individual research tasks can lead to different long-run growth paths.

Reading guide

We begin with the household’s return and then examine what its records teach. Careers follows the price of that learning and the response of formal training, Research carries the resulting expertise into the production of new knowledge, and Welfare brings the private and social accounts together. In the mathematical introduction, we explain how these decisions fit into one equilibrium, while Explore the economy lets us follow their connections directly.
